text: Water early in the morning. Less water evaporates and leaves dry before the afternoon heat.
Push a finger 3 cm into the soil. If it feels dry, water; if it feels damp, wait a day.
More potted plants die from too much water than too little.
Water slowly until it drips from the drainage hole. That means the whole root ball got a drink.
Terracotta pots breathe and dry fast. Plastic pots hold water longer. Adjust your watering to match.
Monsoon tip: tilt pots or raise them on bricks so rainwater never pools at the bottom.
In May heat, small pots on a sunny balcony may need water twice a day.
Save the water used to wash dal and rice. It carries a little nutrition for your plants.
Drip-irrigate for free: poke tiny holes in a bottle cap and turn an old bottle upside down into the pot.
Water the soil, not the leaves. Wet leaves invite fungus, especially in humid cities.
A 3 to 5 cm mulch of dry leaves on top of the soil can cut watering needs noticeably.
RO reject water is salty. Mix it with tap water before using it on plants.
Drooping in the afternoon but fresh by evening? That is heat stress, not thirst.
Grouping pots together raises humidity around them and reduces water loss.
Succulents store water in their leaves. Water deeply but rarely.
Yellow lower leaves plus wet soil usually means overwatering, not hunger.
Self-watering pots with a reservoir are great for people who travel often.
Leaving town for a week? Group your pots in a shady corner standing on a wet towel.
East-facing balconies get gentle morning sun, which most herbs and flowers love.
West-facing balconies get harsh afternoon sun. Pick heat-lovers like bougainvillea and portulaca.
North-facing balconies in India get little direct sun. Ferns, money plant and peace lily do well there.
South-facing balconies are the sunniest in India, ideal for vegetables and fruiting plants.
Fruiting vegetables like tomato and chilli need at least 6 hours of direct sun to give a good harvest.
Leafy greens like palak and methi can manage with 3 to 4 hours of sun.
Count sun hours on a weekend: check your balcony every hour and note where light falls.
A plant leaning toward the window is asking for more light. Rotate it weekly.
A 50% green shade net over the balcony in April and May can save tender plants from scorching.
Pale, stretched stems mean the plant is not getting enough light.
White walls reflect light. A bright wall can add useful light to a shady balcony.
Indoor plants near a window get many times more light than those a few metres inside the room.
In winter the sun is lower and reaches deeper into balconies. Move sun-lovers forward.
A good Indian potting mix: 40% garden soil, 30% compost, 30% cocopeat or sand.
Never use plain garden soil in pots. It compacts and chokes the roots.
Cocopeat holds water like a sponge and keeps pots light, which helps on balconies with weight limits.
Vermicompost is gentle and safe; you can add a handful to every pot each month.
Kitchen waste plus dry leaves in a perforated bin becomes compost in about 6 to 8 weeks.
Banana peels soaked in water for 2 days make a potassium-rich liquid feed for flowering plants.
Crushed eggshells add calcium and help prevent blossom-end rot in tomatoes.
Used tea leaves, rinsed and dried, add organic matter to the soil.
Every pot needs a drainage hole. No hole means rotten roots, sooner or later.
Refresh the top 3 cm of soil in long-lived pots every year to restore nutrients.
Diluted buttermilk (1:10) is a traditional booster that curry leaf and many plants respond to.
Fermented jeevamrut from cow dung, jaggery and besan is a popular natural farming tonic.
Pots heavier than about 50 kg should sit close to walls or beams. Ask your society about balcony load limits.
Grow bags are cheap, light and let roots breathe. Great for vegetables on terraces.
Neem oil spray: 5 ml neem oil plus a few drops of liquid soap in 1 litre of water. Spray at dusk.
White cotton-like patches on hibiscus are mealybugs. Wipe them off with neem oil on a cotton bud.
Curling chilli leaves are often caused by thrips or mites. Check the leaf underside.
Yellow sticky traps catch whiteflies and fungus gnats without chemicals.
Marigolds near vegetables help repel nematodes and some insects.
Ladybirds eat aphids. Dill, coriander flowers and marigold attract them to your balcony.
A strong spray of plain water knocks aphids off stems. Repeat for 3 days.
Check new plants from the nursery for pests before placing them next to your other pots.
Garlic-chilli spray is a classic Indian kitchen pesticide. Blend, strain, dilute and spray.
Monsoon brings snails and fungus. Remove dead leaves and keep pots slightly apart for air flow.
Pigeons digging in pots? A layer of pebbles or a net over the soil keeps them away.
Mosquitoes breed in saucers. Empty plate trays after watering, especially in monsoon.
Add a few guppy fish to your lotus tub. They eat mosquito larvae.
Holes in leaves with no bug in sight? Caterpillars feed at night. Check with a torch.
June to July is the best planting time in most of India. Monsoon rain helps new plants settle.
October to November is perfect for sowing winter vegetables like palak, methi, carrot and peas.
Sow coriander now. Cool weather keeps it leafy for longer before it flowers.
February to March is the time to sow summer crops like bhindi, lauki, cucumber and karela.
Summer survival: shift delicate pots to the shadiest wall and water in the evening as well.
In north Indian winters, cover tulsi with a cloth at night to protect it from frost.
October is rose pruning month. Cut stems by a third for a flush of winter blooms.
Stop pinching chrysanthemum tips by end of August so buds form in time for Diwali.
Sow marigold seeds in September for orange blooms by Diwali.
January is the time to hard-prune mogra for a flood of summer flowers.
Winter is the best season for strawberries, petunias and pansies in the Indian plains.
Before summer, add mulch to every pot. It keeps roots up to several degrees cooler.
Clean drains and gutters before the monsoon so balcony water does not flood the pots.
After the monsoon, give pots a feed of compost. Heavy rain washes nutrients away.
Plants grow slowly in winter. Reduce watering and feeding until spring.
Vegetation can lower local temperatures by a few degrees through shade and evapotranspiration.
Green roofs can hold back a large share of rainfall and slow stormwater runoff.
Indian cities are heat islands. Concrete can stay hot long after sunset, while plants cool the air.
A green curtain of climbers on a west wall can noticeably cool the room behind it.
Every pot of soil stores a little carbon. Thousands of balconies add up.
Growing your own greens cuts the transport, packaging and cold storage behind store-bought vegetables.
Native and drought-hardy plants need far less water, which matters in water-stressed cities.
Composting kitchen waste keeps it out of landfills, where it would release methane.
Plants release water vapour through their leaves, which acts as a natural air conditioner.
A balcony full of plants also traps some street dust on its leaves.
Harvesting rainwater from a balcony pipe into a bucket can water pots for days.
Choosing plants that suit your climate means less water, less fertiliser and fewer failures.
Start with three easy plants. Success with a few beats losing many.
Money plant, snake plant and aloe vera are nearly impossible to kill. Perfect first plants.
Buy from a local nursery when possible. The plants are already used to your city's weather.
Give new plants a week in light shade before moving them into full sun.
Repot only when roots come out of the drainage hole, and go up just one pot size.
Leaves turning yellow is normal for old leaves. Worry only if new leaves yellow.
Write the sowing date on the pot with a marker. It makes harvest timing easy.
Most herbs grow bushier the more you harvest them. Pinch the tips often.
Rotate pots a quarter turn each week so plants grow evenly.
Remove dead flowers (deadheading) and most plants will make more blooms.
Kitchen scraps can regrow: spring onion roots, mint stems, garlic cloves and coriander seeds.
One plant that thrives is better than ten that struggle. Choose for your conditions, not the photo.
Plants sold in tiny nursery bags should be moved to a proper pot within a week or two.
A plant diary or phone photos each week help you spot problems early.
Hanging baskets dry out the fastest. Check them first on hot days.
Put tall plants at the back and trailing plants at the edges of your balcony.
Feed little and often. Too much fertiliser burns roots.
Morning is the best time to inspect plants. Pests and wilting are easiest to spot then.
Tulsi is grown in a tulsi vrindavan in many Indian homes and worshipped every morning.
Red hibiscus is traditionally offered to Lord Ganesha and Goddess Kali.
Marigold torans hang on doors for almost every Indian festival, from Diwali to weddings.
Mogra gajras have scented Indian evenings for centuries.
Parijat is said in legend to have been brought from heaven by Lord Krishna.
Bael leaves in sets of three are offered to Lord Shiva.
Shami leaves are exchanged as 'gold' on Dussehra in Maharashtra.
Many Indian homes keep a money plant for prosperity, as per Vastu belief.
The lotus is India's national flower and a symbol of purity rising from mud.
Balsam (terda) flowers are used in Gauri pooja during Ganeshotsav in Maharashtra.
Aboli flowers are woven into gajras across Maharashtra and South India.
Aparajita flowers are offered to Lord Shiva and Goddess Durga, and also make a blue tea.
The peepal tree is sacred in Hinduism and Buddhism. The Buddha attained enlightenment under one.
The banyan is India's national tree, known for roots that grow down from its branches.
Amla Navami celebrates the amla tree with a meal eaten beneath it.
During Navratri many homes sow jowar or wheat in a pot as a symbol of prosperity.
The betel leaf (paan) is used in almost every Hindu pooja and welcome ritual.
No South Indian tadka is complete without curry leaves.
A sunflower bud tracks the sun across the sky. Once it opens it usually faces east.
Portulaca is called the 9 O'Clock flower because its blooms open mid-morning.
Dragon fruit flowers bloom for just one night and wilt by morning.
Raat ki rani releases its scent at night to attract moths for pollination.
Parijat flowers fall to the ground before sunrise, which is why it is also called the tree of sorrow.
Snake plants use a special type of photosynthesis that lets them save water.
Aloe vera leaves are about 95% water.
Tulsi has been part of Ayurvedic practice for thousands of years.
Mint spreads through underground runners, which is why it takes over shared pots.
Lotus leaves repel water so well that droplets roll off carrying dust. Scientists call it the lotus effect.
Calathea leaves fold up at night and open in the morning, earning it the name prayer plant.
Bees see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that are invisible to us.
Plants can't move, but they can sense touch, gravity and light.
A single tomato plant in a sunny pot can produce several kilograms of fruit in a season.
Moringa leaves are rich in iron, calcium and vitamin C, earning it the name miracle tree.
Some bamboos are among the fastest-growing plants on Earth.
Papaya can go from seed to fruit in under a year.
Ripe balsam pods burst open when touched, flinging seeds away. That gives it the name touch-me-not.
Plants talk to each other through chemical signals and fungal networks in the soil.
Roots grow toward water and away from light. Plant scientists call it tropism.
A drooping peace lily recovers within hours of watering. It is a built-in thirst alarm.
About one in every three bites of food we eat depends on pollinators.
India is one of the world's megadiverse countries, home to a large share of global plant species.
Curry leaf belongs to the citrus family, the same family as lemon.
Coriander leaves and dhania seeds come from the same plant.
One balcony is small. Thousands of balconies are an urban forest.
If 10% of homes greened just 2 square metres each, a city would gain hectares of new green space.
Flowering plants on your balcony are fuel stations for bees and butterflies in the city.
A pot of tulsi or marigold can attract pollinators to an otherwise concrete floor.
Growing even a few herbs at home cuts down on plastic packaging from the market.
Sunbirds and bulbuls visit balconies with nectar flowers like ixora, pentas and hibiscus.
Shared seedlings build neighbourhoods. Swap cuttings with your society members.
Kitchen gardens connect children to where food comes from.
A green view from your window has been linked to lower stress.
Every kilogram of food you grow is a kilogram that didn't need a truck.
A diverse balcony with herbs, flowers and climbers supports more insects than one type of plant.
Community gardens on terraces in Mumbai and Pune now grow vegetables for whole buildings.

No results. Try searching in Hindi or Marathi, like tulsi, pudina or jaswand.
Quiet here. Plants grow in silence too, then one morning there's a flower.
A 60 cm trough of methi or palak can give a family a bunch of greens every week.
Harvest leafy greens from the outside in. The centre keeps producing.
Pick chillies green for heat and freshness, or let them turn red for drying.
Microgreens are ready in 7 to 12 days and can hold more nutrients than mature leaves.
Pick tomatoes when they blush pink and let them ripen indoors. Birds won't get them first.
Harvest bhindi every other day. Pods left too long turn woody.
Sow leafy greens every two weeks in small batches for a continuous harvest.
Herbs taste strongest just before they flower. That is the best time to harvest.
A lemon tree in a large pot can give dozens of lemons a year.
Vertical gardening lets climbers like karela and cucumber use the wall instead of the floor.
Crops that need hand pollination on high-rise balconies include gourds and pumpkins. Few bees reach the 15th floor.
Snip whole curry leaf sprigs instead of single leaves. The plant becomes bushier.
Use every layer: floor pots, railing planters, wall shelves and hanging baskets.
A balcony railing planter can hold a row of herbs without using any floor space.
Climbers turn bare walls and grills into green screens for privacy.
Trailing plants like portulaca and money plant soften hard concrete edges.
Tiered plant stands give each pot its own light.
A 1.8 m by 1.2 m balcony can comfortably hold 8 to 12 pots arranged in layers.
Keep the heaviest pots near walls and the lightest ones on railings and hooks.
Leave a 60 cm walkway. You need room to water, prune and sit with your chai.
Window sills are perfect for herbs. Just make sure pots are secured against wind.
Use saucers under balcony pots so water doesn't drip onto the neighbours below.
